solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Parasite running me lower

indicators.note: colours that are running blur and spread out of place, so the letters move about freely

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters to rework

explanation.surface: A parasite is draining someone and making them feel lower and lower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running me lower' reads like a complaint about being run down, but it is the whole of the wordplay: EELWORM is a rearrangement of ME LOWER.
explanation.definitionFit: Eelworms are tiny nematodes that live off plants or animals, a textbook example of a parasitic organism.

clue.text: What detects supporters abandoning Oxford college

indicators.note: whatever is abandoning a place walks out of it, so those letters leave the larger word

parts.note: Brasenose is a college of Oxford University
bras are garments that support

explanation.surface: A sniffer device notices fans walking away from an Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: Brasenose College loses its opening BRAS to leave E-NOSE; 'supporters' wants to mean fans, but it is underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic nose is a sensor array built to detect and identify smells, so it is literally a thing that detects.

clue.text: Spicy dish involved cheese got around Hackney

indicators.note: to get around something is to go about it on all sides, so one piece encloses the other
something involved is tangled and convoluted, so its letters are knotted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a hackney carriage is a taxi, a cab

explanation.surface: A spicy dish of rearranged cheese was served around Hackney, in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney looks like the London borough, but it is the old hackney carriage, a CAB, which goes inside ES-ECHE, the shuffled cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Escabeche is a Spanish and Latin American dish of fish or meat marinated in a sharp, spiced vinegar sauce.

clue.text: Dance around very old dovecote

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece is placed outside the other

parts.note: a loure is a slow French dance
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: People dance around a very old dovecote on a village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very old' looks like one phrase, but 'very' gives V and 'old' belongs to the definition, marking an obsolete sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers records louvre in an obsolete sense of a dovecote, from the slatted turret that let birds and smoke through.

clue.text: Suppose mine's missing money after work

parts.note: OP, short for opus, is a work

indicators.note: a thing that is missing is absent, so those letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: taken as written; the apostrophe-s is 'is'
M is an abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: Someone supposes their mine has lost money once the work is done.
explanation.walkthrough: MINE loses M, and the leftover INE comes after OP, the opus abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To opine is to express or hold an opinion, much as supposing is offering a view without proof.

clue.text: Encountered a small carnivore, one canine having alternate life cycle

parts.note: met means encountered
taken as written
a genet is a small cat-like carnivore
I is the Roman numeral one
C is an abbreviation for canine, as a tooth

explanation.surface: Someone met a small carnivore and a dog, a creature with an odd life cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces strung in order; 'canine' looks like a dog but gives only its abbreviation C, as in dental notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Metagenesis is alternation of generations, where sexual and asexual stages take turns through an organism's life history.

clue.text: Planktonic creature covered over in metaplasm

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the letters are read backwards
what is covered lies beneath an outer layer, so the letters sit inside other words

parts.note: the run of letters in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A tiny marine creature is coated with metaplasm, the non-living stuff of a cell.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'metaplasm' and are read backwards; 'in' here just links the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A salpa, or salp, is a barrel-shaped tunicate that drifts in the open sea as part of the plankton.

clue.text: Eastern European dance endlessly coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top
without an end means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: valse is the French form of waltz, a dance

explanation.surface: An Eastern European dance keeps on coming round without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern European dance' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at 'European'; VALSE loses its E and climbs the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Slavs are the peoples of Eastern Europe speaking Slavic languages, such as Poles, Czechs and Russians.

clue.text: Exactly dividing area Lima and Quito demolished

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: a demolished structure is knocked down and rebuilt in some other form

parts.note: Lima is L in the NATO alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: An area split exactly between Lima and Quito, two South American capitals, has been knocked down.
explanation.walkthrough: Lima looks like Peru's capital beside Ecuador's, but it is the radio code word for L; only Quito is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: An aliquot part divides a whole an exact number of times with no remainder, as 3 does 12.

clue.text: Left with mostly creamy white, black and blue coloration

indicators.note: most but not all of a word means its final letter is dropped

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
ivory is a creamy white colour

explanation.surface: A paint scheme mixing creamy white with black and blue.
explanation.walkthrough: The colours look like a palette, but 'black and blue' means bruised; IVORY is docked of its Y after L.
explanation.definitionFit: Livor is the livid bluish discoloration of skin, as from bruising or after death, so it is a bruise colour.

clue.text: Once favoured emperor returned in maturity

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: age is maturity, as in 'come of age'

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a tsar was a Russian emperor

explanation.surface: A once-favoured emperor comes back to power in his mature years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word: AGRASTE is Spenser's past tense of agrace, to favour, so the clue's first two words are the definition rather than part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser used agraste as the past tense of agrace, meaning showed grace or favour to, so it is an archaic synonym.

clue.text: Gushing, noisy and reckless prime minister doubly out of fashion

indicators.note: out of means removed from, and doubly says the removal happens to two words

parts.note: a ton-up boy was a noisy, reckless biker who rode at 100 mph
the Duke of Wellington was a British prime minister
ton is an old word for fashion, the fashionable set

explanation.surface: A noisy, reckless prime minister is twice judged unfashionable and over the top.
explanation.walkthrough: TON is removed from both TON-UP and WELLINGTON. Ton-up describes 1950s–60s British motorcyclists who did a 'ton' (100 mph).
explanation.definitionFit: Upwelling describes liquid rising and flowing out from below, which is close to a gushing stream.

clue.text: Warning I've broadcast about European condiment

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece sits outside another
seed that is broadcast is scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rework
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A broadcaster gives a warning about some European food product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warning' looks like the start of an announcement, but it and 'I've' supply all but one letter; the single E slips into the rearranged string.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine vinegar is vinegar made from fermented wine, used as a seasoning and dressing on the table.

clue.text: Windows left out of small chambers

indicators.note: taking something out of a word removes it, leaving the rest behind

parts.note: loculi are small compartments or cells
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Windows have been left out of some small rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb, 'left out', but it is the letter L, removed from LOCULI.
explanation.definitionFit: An oculus is a round eye-like window, as in a dome or church wall, so the Latin plural names such windows.

clue.text: Rave in Troon initially? Could be

definitions.text: Rave in Troon initially? Could be

indicators.note: could be suggests a possible alternative form, so the letters may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a rave might take place in the Scottish town of Troon.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: TAIVER is a Scots word for raving or wandering in talk, and Troon is a town on the Ayrshire coast, so the word is what a rave would be there.
explanation.definitionFit: Taiver is a Scots verb meaning to wander or rave in speech, so it is the regional equivalent of rave.

clue.text: A vehicle new in South America pampas?

definitions.note: pampas is plural; the question mark marks savanna as an example of such grassland

indicators.note: to be in something is to be held within it, so those letters sit inside another piece

parts.note: SA is the abbreviation for South America
taken as written
a van is a vehicle
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A new vehicle out on the South American plains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South America' looks like scenery, but SA is split to hold the rest; the question mark admits that pampas are only one kind of savanna.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are the treeless grassy plains of Argentina, much like the savanna grasslands of Africa, so savanna is a near equivalent.

clue.text: One managing land business set up very like upper crust

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up stands it on end, so the letters read upward

parts.note: bus. is an abbreviation for business
V is the abbreviation for very
as means like
sal, or sial, is the geologists' name for the upper layer of the earth's crust

explanation.surface: A land management business is set up in a very upper-class way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper crust' looks like the aristocracy, but it is geology: sal is a variant of sial, the silicon- and aluminium-rich rock of the upper crust.
explanation.definitionFit: A subvassal holds land from a vassal, who holds it from a lord, so he is someone who holds and works an estate under feudal tenure.

clue.text: River of York half on the turn

indicators.note: on the turn means turning round, and half limits that turn to one part of the word

parts.note: Ebor, from the Latin Eboracum, is the traditional abbreviation for York, as in the Archbishop's signature

explanation.surface: Half of a river in York is turning with the tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River of York' looks like the Ouse, but 'of' only links; Ebor for York is a convention from the Archbishop of York's signature and the Ebor horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ebro is the longest river entirely within Spain, flowing into the Mediterranean in Catalonia.

clue.text: Eastern draught ox that was wild on earth

indicators.note: in an across entry, sitting on something means following after it

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earth
the urus, or aurochs, was the extinct wild ox

explanation.surface: An eastern draught ox, once wild, is now working the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draught ox' looks like a single idea, a beast that pulls a plough, but 'draught' belongs to the definition as a current of air.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurus is the Greek god of the east wind, and a draught is a current of air, so this is a classical name for an easterly.

clue.text: I refuse to accept mark of the beast on sides of bare earth building in Mycenae

indicators.note: in an across entry, sitting on something means coming after it
the sides of a word are its two edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: the outside letters of this word
the outside letters of this word
to veto is to refuse to accept, so I + VETO
the initials of mark and beast, M and B

explanation.surface: A believer refuses the mark of the beast, the sign of the Antichrist in Revelation, on bare ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The apocalyptic surface hides plain letter work; 'on' puts the edge letters first, and the definition sits at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: The great tholos tombs of Mycenae, such as the Treasury of Atreus, are domed stone burial chambers shaped like old straw hives.

clue.text: Digitally mark beat with piano lacking bass

indicators.note: lacking one thing in favour of another means one letter is swapped out for a different one

parts.note: bethump is an old word meaning to thump soundly
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
B is the abbreviation for bass

explanation.surface: A musician marks the beat with a piano that has no bass notes.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface hides two music abbreviations: P for piano is swapped for B for bass at the end of BETHUMP.
explanation.definitionFit: To bethumb is to mark a book with the thumbs by heavy handling, and digits are fingers and thumbs, so this is a witty definition.

clue.text: Big Issue up north, somewhat extreme in opinion

parts.note: high means big, as in a high price
ish is a Scots legal word for issue, an exit or expiry

explanation.surface: A magazine sold in northern streets carries rather extreme views.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Issue is a British magazine sold by homeless vendors; here the words split, and 'up north' marks a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: High describes an extreme view, as in high Tory or high church, and the suffix softens it to somewhat.

clue.text: Accusatory, inventing things, I am popular for eccentricity

indicators.note: one thing given for another is a swap, so new letters take the place of old ones

parts.note: creative people invent things
I'M plus IN, which means popular
e is the symbol for eccentricity in mathematics

explanation.surface: An accuser says an inventive person is popular only for being eccentric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentricity' looks like a quirk of character, but it is e, the eccentricity of a conic, replaced inside CREATIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminative means charging someone with a crime, the same as an accusatory statement levelled at a suspect.

clue.text: Rainbow-coloured flags, final three raised

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters reads them upward, and final three limits that to the tail

parts.note: flags are irises, and irides is a plural of iris

explanation.surface: Rainbow flags are hoisted, the last three run up the pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flags' looks like banners, but it is the iris plant; its plural must be the less familiar IRIDES for the reversal to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris was the Greek goddess of the rainbow, and irised means showing rainbow colours, iridescent.

clue.text: Murderous behaviour of eastern people holding good

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it within one's grasp, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the Thai are a people of South-East Asia
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Murderous conduct among an eastern people who nonetheless hold to the good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' only links; THAGI is a variant spelling of thuggee, the practice of the Thugs of India.
explanation.definitionFit: Thuggee was ritual murder and robbery by Indian gangs of stranglers, the origin of the word thug.

clue.text: Goad a natural killer oneself

parts.note: taken as written
NK stands for natural killer, a kind of immune cell
us can refer to oneself, as in the informal 'give us a look'

explanation.surface: Someone urges a natural-born killer to act alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural killer' sounds like a born murderer, but it is the medical NK cell.
explanation.definitionFit: An ankus is the hooked stick used in India to drive and steer elephants, so it is a kind of prod.

clue.text: Sober Hindu out of India?

parts.note: sad in its old sense of serious, sober

indicators.note: a thing taken out of a word is removed from it

parts.note: taken as written
IND is the abbreviation for India

explanation.surface: A serious-minded Hindu travels outside India.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a sadhu is a sober, ascetic Hindu, and the question mark admits he is rarely out of India.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadhu is a Hindu holy man who renounces worldly life, so sober and ascetic describes him well.

clue.text: Scotland's apart relatively to brother English

parts.note: Fra is the title of an Italian friar, a brother
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Scotland stands apart from its English brother.
explanation.walkthrough: The long first half is all definition: 'apart relatively to' is a roundabout way of saying from, and Scotland's version of that preposition is frae.
explanation.definitionFit: From expresses separation relative to something, as in apart from, and frae is the Scots spelling.

clue.text: Your aged relative is turning abrasive

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: yr is the written abbreviation for your
eme is an archaic word for an uncle

explanation.surface: Your elderly relative is becoming rather abrasive in old age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abrasive' looks like a description of the relative's manner, but it is the definition; 'aged' marks the obsolete word EME.
explanation.definitionFit: Emery is a hard rock powder used on boards and paper for grinding and polishing, a classic abrasive material.

clue.text: Enthusiastic about popular couple reportedly

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so a sound stands in for a spelling

parts.note: a couple is two, which sounds like the preposition

explanation.surface: Fans are keen on a popular celebrity couple, so the gossip says.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second piece is a sound-alike; 'popular' gives IN directly.
explanation.definitionFit: Being into something is the informal idiom for being keen on it or a fan of it.

clue.text: Thus interrupting friend over style of pronunciation

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the letters run backwards
to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a mate is a friend
sic is Latin for thus

explanation.surface: Butting in on a friend to correct the way they speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thus' is the Latin word printed in brackets after a quoted error. The insertion happens first and the whole string is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Etacism is pronouncing the Greek letter eta like the English long a or e, a particular way of saying Greek.

clue.text: Remove monarch's power, throwing out with no justice

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: junking means throwing out as rubbish
J is the abbreviation for justice, a judge

explanation.surface: Revolutionaries strip a king of power, expelling him without a fair trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throwing out' looks like the act of deposing, part of the story, but it supplies the word that loses J.
explanation.definitionFit: To unking is to depose, depriving a ruler of the crown and royal authority.

clue.text: Where poet once wrote trifle? That's not right

indicators.note: not means without, so those letters are removed

parts.note: a trifle, the layered pudding, is a dessert
RT is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Did the poet once write a trifle, some slight piece? That seems wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifle' looks like a slight poem, but it is the British layered pudding; 'poet' here is Spenser, whose word desse meant a desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Desse is Spenser's spelling of desk, the place where a writer sits to compose.

clue.text: Charlie, perhaps has to feel pain without oxygen

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: must means has to
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
to ache is to feel pain

explanation.surface: Charlie has to suffer without enough oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but here it means outside. Charlie Chaplin's toothbrush moustache was his trademark, hence the 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Chaplin's small clipped moustache is so famous that a charlie is an example of that facial hair.

clue.text: Attack over poet

parts.note: to bash is to attack
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A critic launches an attack on a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like 'about', but it is O from cricket scorecards, where an over is a set of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: Matsuo Basho was the seventeenth-century Japanese master of haiku, a famous example of a poet.

clue.text: Rector deeply missing professor, frankly

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for rector

indicators.note: a thing that is missing is absent, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: profoundly means deeply
prof is short for professor

explanation.surface: A rector deeply misses a professor and says so plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing' looks like longing for someone, but it removes letters from the word for deeply.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak roundly is to speak bluntly and without mincing words, the same as speaking frankly.
